about: Sønderborg's connecting words for the café world (docs/roadmap/cafe-world.md section 3): the words a city teaches outside its 100 cards.

Derived from two sources and checked by city1-connecting-words.test.ts: the ledger forms in src/lang/da/curriculum-support.ts whose first stage is city 0 (taught as productive-target or preview-as-chunk, or heard as receptive-ambient), plus every targetSpan of src/data/city1-review-upgrade.da.json. "okay" is left out (the same word in English).

Added by the owner on 2026-10-04: skål, om and hen. The ledger (src/lang/da/curriculum-support.ts) stages them at city 0 too, but only as receptive-ambient: heard in City 1, not taught, with no coverage floor. They were left out of the first 44 for that reason; the owner added them, making 47. Their from is ledger-city0-heard (ledger-city0 stays the taught forms), ledger records the stage, and addedBy records the decision.

en.shown is the short English on the tag; en.keys are every English meaning. Two words whose keys overlap are never offered against each other. kind is the pool for "same kind of word" wrong answers (greeting, question, little-word); pos is the finer word class.

meaning.source: city1-review-upgrade = the accepted meaningEn of that file (owner-approved 2026-09-26); cafe-world-prototype = written in the planning session for docs/design/cafe-world/build-door-dash-data.py, not reviewed. needsDanishReview marks every meaning a Danish speaker has not checked.

de is the German meaning for players whose app language is German (the src/i18n/glosses/da.de.json role). source lexicon.da.de.json = taken from that file; cw-14 / cw-14b = written for this list (cw-14b for the three added on 2026-10-04). The owner (native German) should read them.

fr, pl, pt, sv and zh are the meanings for players whose app language is French, Polish, European Portuguese, Swedish or Chinese (simplified), the other languages with a complete gloss overlay (COMPLETE in src/i18n/glosses/index.ts). Same shape as de. source lexicon.da.<lang>.json = taken from that file because its gloss is the course sense; cw-14c = written for this list (2026-10-04), with lexicon recording that file's gloss where it differs from the one shown, and note giving the reason for a hard choice. needsOwnerReview marks that no native speaker has read them (src/i18n/REVIEW.md). es, hu, nb and nl have none: their board tags are still English, so their connecting tags are too.

audio.key is the clip under public/audio/da/: audio/da/<key>.mp3. audio.spoken is what the voice was asked to say; five bare words came back near-silent (en, et, ja, i dag, and om in the 2026-10-04 batch), so they were said as one-word sentences.

fr.note: hej is the informal greeting: salut. lexicon.da.fr.json has bonjour, kept as a key.

meaning.reviewNote: Rather formal in Danish; everyday greeting is hej.

pt.note: Literally good day; Danish goddag is said at any hour, so boa tarde is a key too.

zh.note: The polite 您好 for the rather formal goddag.

fr.note: French says bonjour in the morning. The bracket tells it from goddag on the tag; the keys drop it, so the two are never offered against each other.

pl.note: Polish says dzień dobry in the morning. The bracket tells it from goddag on the tag; the keys drop it.

pt.note: Bom dia is the morning greeting. The bracket tells it from goddag (also bom dia) on the tag; the keys drop it.

meaning.reviewNote: In Danish mostly on the phone or to get attention; check that "hello" does not overstate it.

fr.note: Danish hallo is mostly the phone or calling for attention: allô.

pl.note: Polish halo is the phone and calling for attention, as Danish hallo.

pt.note: Phone and calling for attention. Alô leans Brazilian; a Portuguese speaker answers the phone with "Estou?". A reader should choose.

zh.note: 喂 is the phone hello and calling for attention, as Danish hallo.

sv.note: Danish farvel is the everyday goodbye; Swedish adjö (lexicon.da.sv.json) is formal and old-fashioned, so hej då is shown and adjö kept as a key.

pl.note: The tag is thank you, so dziękuję; lexicon.da.pl.json has the informal dzięki, kept as a key.

fr.note: lexicon.da.fr.json has the noun excuse, not the word said.

zh.note: lexicon.da.zh.json has 道歉 (to apologise), the verb, not the word said.

pl.note: Polish tak (yes) is spelled like Danish tak (thanks), and both are greetings here, so a gate asking ja can show the tag tak with the suitcase tak as a wrong answer. A false friend, kept because tak is the Polish word.

zh.note: lexicon.da.zh.json has 是, which alone also reads as "to be"; 是的 is the answer yes.

meaning.reviewNote: Also "how" in exclamations ("Hvor er det godt!").

pt.note: European Portuguese writes porquê standing alone and porque at the head of a question.

pl.note: lexicon.da.pl.json has mało (little, too little), the other sense; lidt here is a little: trochę.

pt.note: lexicon.da.pt.json has poucos (few); lidt here is a little: um pouco.

zh.note: lexicon.da.zh.json has 少量 (a small amount), a written word; 一点 is what is said.

meaning.reviewNote: Also the "der" of "der er" (there is) and a relative "who/that".

zh.note: lexicon.da.zh.json has 只有, kept as a key; 只 alone is the adverb.

fr.note: The tag is very (the English shown); lexicon.da.fr.json has beaucoup, kept as a key, which also keeps it apart from mange.

pl.note: The tag is very; lexicon.da.pl.json has dużo, kept as a key.

zh.note: The tag is very; lexicon.da.zh.json has 很多, kept as a key.

fr.note: The course sense is the adverb really; lexicon.da.fr.json has the adjective réel.

pl.note: The course sense is the adverb really; lexicon.da.pl.json has the adjective prawdziwy.

pt.note: The course sense is the adverb really; lexicon.da.pt.json has the adjective real.

sv.note: The course sense is the adverb really; lexicon.da.sv.json has the adjective verklig.

zh.note: The course sense is really; lexicon.da.zh.json has 真实 (real, true).

fr.note: lexicon.da.fr.json has the noun retour; the adverb is de retour.

zh.note: Chinese has no one preposition for without; 没有 is the plainest ("without milk": 没有牛奶). It also reads "not have".
Chinese verbs have no past tense; the tag names the past of 是.

fr.note: May, be allowed to. French pouvoir is both may and can, so it is a key of må and kan alike and the two are never offered against each other.

pl.note: May, be allowed to. lexicon.da.pl.json has móc, which is also can; it is a key of må and kan alike.

pt.note: May, be allowed to. lexicon.da.pt.json has poder, which is also can; it is a key of må and kan alike.

meaning.reviewNote: Taught at city 0 only inside chunks ("Kan jeg få …?"); the modal itself comes at city 7.

zh.note: 可以 is both may and can, so it is a key of kan and må alike.

meaning.reviewNote: Also the number one; shown as "a".

fr.note: Danish en/et (common/neuter) do not line up with French un/une; both show un, as the English shows a for both.

pl.note: Polish has no articles. Danish en/et are also the number one, so both show jeden.

zh.note: Chinese has no articles; 一个 (one, a) for both en and et.

meaning.reviewNote: Also the number one; shown as "a".
Also "that", and "the" before an adjective ("den røde dør"); shown as "it".

fr.note: Den stands for a common-gender thing; French says il or elle by the noun.

pl.note: Den stands for a common-gender thing; Polish says on or ona by the noun.

meaning.reviewNote: Also "that", and "the" before an adjective ("det store hus"); shown as "it".
Lower-case "i" is "in"; capital "I" is "you" (plural). Shown as "in".
The toast. Also the noun "skål" (bowl), which this list does not mean.

de.note: lexicon.da.de.json glosses skål as the noun "Schüssel" (bowl), not the toast, so it is not used here.

fr.note: lexicon.da.fr.json glosses skål as the noun bol (bowl), not the toast.

pl.note: lexicon.da.pl.json glosses skål as the noun miska (bowl), not the toast.

pt.note: lexicon.da.pt.json glosses skål as the noun tigela (bowl), not the toast.

sv.note: Swedish skål is the toast as well as the bowl, as in Danish; the toast is meant here.

zh.note: lexicon.da.zh.json glosses skål as the noun 碗 (bowl), not the toast.

addedBy.note: Heard in City 1, not taught (ledger receptive-ambient); added to the connecting words by the owner.

meaning.reviewNote: The prototype lists it twice: preposition "about" and conjunction "whether | if". Also "in" with time ("om en time"). Shown as "about".

addedBy.note: Heard in City 1, not taught (ledger receptive-ambient); added to the connecting words by the owner.

meaning.reviewNote: A direction word, rarely alone: "gå hen til" (go over to), "Hvor skal du hen?" (where are you going?). Shown as "over to".

fr.note: A direction word: "gå hen til" is aller vers, s'approcher de.

pl.note: A direction word: "gå hen til" is podejść do.

pt.note: A direction word: "gå hen til døren" is ir até à porta.

sv.note: A direction word: "gå hen til" is gå fram till; "Hvor skal du hen?" is "Vart ska du?".

zh.note: A direction word: "gå hen til" is 走过去. 过去 alone also reads "the past".

addedBy.note: Heard in City 1, not taught (ledger receptive-ambient); added to the connecting words by the owner.
